# Interactive sessions and GPU jobs {#sec-interactive}

::: {.tldr}
For hands-on work, `salloc` gives you a live shell on a compute node (start it inside `tmux`
so a dropped connection doesn't kill it). For GPUs, add `--gres=gpu:N` and pick a GPU
partition — develop on cheap **A30s** (start in minutes), reserve **H100s** for jobs that
truly need them (start in hours). GPU CUDA work needs the deprecated `gcc/13.2.0`.
:::

## Interactive sessions with `salloc` {#sec-salloc}

When you need to poke at things by hand — debug a crash, explore a dataset, build and test a
model interactively — request an interactive allocation:

```bash
salloc --account=cowy-firesurro --qos=interactive \
       --time=02:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=16G
```

`salloc` requires at least `--account` and `--time`. When it grants the allocation you get a
shell **on a compute node** — now you can run heavy things freely, because you're no longer on
the login node. The `interactive` QOS is tuned for exactly this: it starts in ~10–30 seconds
(@sec-queue-times) with an 8-hour ceiling.

::: {.callout-important}
## Launch `salloc` from inside `tmux`
An interactive session lives in *your shell*. If your laptop sleeps or WiFi drops, the shell
dies and the session ends. Start `tmux` on the login node **first**, then `salloc` inside it
(@sec-tmux). Now you can detach, close the laptop, and reattach tomorrow with the session
intact — as long as it's within your `--time`.
:::

When you're done, `exit` the shell to release the allocation (don't sit on idle cores — it
hurts your fair-share and blocks others).

### Interactive apps in the portal

The web portal (@sec-first-login) offers graphical interactive apps — a full XFCE desktop,
**RStudio**, and almost certainly **Jupyter** — that launch as scheduled jobs behind the
scenes. These are the friendliest way to do interactive/GPU notebook work without wrangling
`salloc` and port-forwarding by hand.

## GPU jobs {#sec-gpu}

Request GPUs with `--gres=gpu:<count>` and target a GPU partition:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s          # or mb-h100, mb-a30, ...
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                 # one GPU on the node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8            # CPUs to feed the GPU
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00

module purge
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1   # CUDA needs gcc 13.2, see below
nvidia-smi                                    # confirm the GPU is visible
python train.py
```

To request a **specific GPU type** you can also use the typed form,
e.g. `--gres=gpu:h100:2` for two H100s on one node.

### Which GPU partition? Match it to the phase of work

| GPU partition | GPUs | Typical wait | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mb-a30` | 8× A30 | minutes | **development, proof-of-concept, debugging** |
| `mb-a6000` / `mb-r6000` | 4× each | short–moderate | GPU dev, mid-size jobs |
| `mb-l40s` | 8× L40S | ~1 h+ | inference, mid-size training |
| `mb-h100` | 8× H100 | seconds–**hours** | **large training / production only** |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Don't develop on H100s
H100 nodes are the most contended resource on the machine — waits of several hours are normal
when they're busy (@sec-queue-times). Do your iterate-fast development on **A30s**, which you
can usually get in minutes, and only submit to `mb-h100` when you have a real training run
that needs that horsepower. Check `gpuavail` and `showpartitions` before choosing.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The GPU compiler quirk
`cuda-toolkit` is built only against **`gcc/13.2.0`**, even though `gcc/13.2.0` prints a
deprecation warning nudging you to `gcc/14.2.0`. For GPU/CUDA work, load `gcc/13.2.0` anyway
and ignore the warning (@sec-modules). Inside containers, add `--nv` to expose the GPU
(@sec-conda).
:::

### Checking GPU availability and usage

```bash
gpuavail                    # ARCC helper: free GPUs by type, right now
slurm_gpustat               # cluster-wide GPU utilization
sinfo -p mb-h100 -o "%P %t %G %D"   # H100 node states this second
nvidia-smi                  # inside a GPU job: is my code actually using the GPU?
nvtop                       # inside a GPU job: live GPU usage, like htop for GPUs
```

If `nvidia-smi` shows 0% utilization while your job runs, your code isn't actually on the GPU
— a common and expensive mistake. Verify early.
